before_full_plan_page.title: Euclidean Ordinary Differential Equations with Smooth Dependence

items.title: The variational equation along an ODE solution
Linear matrix ODEs have unique global solutions on a fixed interval
items.strategy: Extend the coefficient field to an open time interval, view an $n \times n$ matrix as a vector in $\mathbb R^{n^2}$, and apply Picard-Lindelof locally. The Volterra equation, norm-integral estimate, and Gronwall bound control both time directions, and the continuation theorem prevents finite-endpoint breakdown inside the interval.

items.title: A fundamental matrix is invertible
items.strategy: Solve the inverse linear equation and differentiate the product of a candidate inverse with the fundamental matrix. Uniqueness for the identity-valued solution forces the product to stay equal to the identity.

items.title: $C^1$ dependence of solutions on initial data
items.strategy: Difference quotients satisfy a linearized integral equation. The linear comparison estimate and continuous dependence from the published Picard-Lindelof page drive those difference quotients to the solution of the variational equation.

items.title: Smooth dependence of solutions on initial data
items.strategy: Differentiate the Volterra integral equation inductively. At each order the new highest derivative solves an inhomogeneous linear ODE with coefficients built from lower-order derivatives already known to be smooth.

items.title: Smooth dependence of ODE solutions on parameters
items.strategy: Adjoin the parameter as a constant extra variable and reduce the parameter-dependent system to the autonomous initial-data theorem. The common local interval is carried through the augmented system rather than assumed silently.

items.title: A bounded vector field on all of Euclidean space is complete
items.strategy: The integral equation bounds the displacement by the bound on the speed times the elapsed time. A finite maximal endpoint therefore cannot force escape from every compact subset of $\mathbb R^n$, contradicting the published continuation criterion.

items.title: A compactly supported smooth Euclidean vector field is complete
items.strategy: A smooth vector field that vanishes outside a compact subset is bounded on that compact set and zero elsewhere. The previous corollary then gives global existence.

items.title: The fundamental theorem for autonomous smooth ODEs
items.strategy: Combine the published Picard-Lindelof existence and uniqueness theorem with the smooth dependence theorem on a common local interval. The result is stated on the honest open domain of triples where the maximal solution exists.

items.title: The fundamental theorem for nonautonomous smooth ODEs
items.strategy: Adjoin the time variable with $\dot s = 1$ and rewrite the nonautonomous system as an autonomous one in one higher dimension. Apply the autonomous theorem and project back to the original variables.

items.title: The maximal solution domain is open
items.strategy: Take a point where a maximal solution exists, move to the corresponding point on its graph, and apply the local fundamental theorem around that point. The resulting common existence neighborhood propagates existence and smoothness to a whole open set of triples.

items.title: Solutions compose under a change of initial time
items.strategy: Both sides solve the same initial value problem at the intermediate time, so uniqueness on the common domain identifies them. The open-domain proposition ensures the equality is stated exactly where both expressions make sense.

items.title: A smooth Euclidean vector field need not be complete
items.strategy: The scalar equation $\dot x = x^2$ has a smooth right-hand side but the solution from $x(0)=1$ blows up at time $1$. Smoothness does not control growth at infinity.

items.title: Pointwise local existence does not force one global uniform time interval
items.strategy: Uniform time intervals are local in the initial data, not global over all of $\mathbb R^n$. A family of initial conditions moving toward faster and faster blow-up witnesses the failure.

items.title: A maximal ODE solution need not have a closed interval domain
items.strategy: Maximal domains are open intervals because local existence always extends a solution a little away from an interior point. Finite-time blow-up produces a maximal domain of the form $(-\infty,1)$ or $(a,b)$ rather than a closed interval.

items.title: Continuous dependence does not by itself imply differentiable dependence
items.strategy: Differentiable dependence uses derivatives of the vector field and the variational equation. Continuous dependence from Picard-Lindelof is strictly weaker than the smooth-dependence block built on this page.
